claim: A prolonged TB therapy is primarily responsible for development of drug resistance by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb).
source: A prolonged therapy, primarily responsible for development of drug resistance by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), obligates any new TB regimen to not only reduce treatment duration but also escape pathogen resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as background context in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Sertraline (SRT) stunts the pro-pathogenic type I IFN response of macrophages to Mtb infection.
source: With the aim of harnessing the host response in providing support to existing regimens, we used sertraline (SRT) to stunt the pro-pathogenic type I IFN response of macrophages to infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent inhibition of type I IFN response in Figure 1A-B.

claim: SRT alone could only arrest bacterial growth in macrophages.
source: While SRT alone could only arrest bacterial growth, it effectively escalated the bactericidal activities of Isoniazid (H) and Rifampicin (R) in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1C showing bacterial stasis with SRT treatment.

claim: SRT effectively escalated the bactericidal activities of Isoniazid (H) and Rifampicin (R) in macrophages.
source: While SRT alone could only arrest bacterial growth, it effectively escalated the bactericidal activities of Isoniazid (H) and Rifampicin (R) in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1D-E showing enhanced bacterial killing with HRS combination.

claim: The strengthening of antibiotic potencies by SRT was more evident in conditions of ineffective control by frontline TB drugs, against tolerant strains or dormant Mtb.
source: This strengthening of antibiotic potencies by SRT was more evident in conditions of ineffective control by these frontline TB drug, against tolerant strains or dormant Mtb.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1G-H showing enhanced efficacy in vitamin C-treated and lipid-rich macrophages, and Figure 7 showing efficacy against tolerant strains.

claim: SRT could significantly combine with standard TB drugs to enhance early pathogen clearance from tissues of mice infected with either drug sensitive/tolerant strains of Mtb.
source: SRT, could significantly combine with standard TB drugs to enhance early pathogen clearance from tissues of mice infected with either drug sensitive/tolerant strains of Mtb.
evidence: Supported by in vivo data in Figures 4-7 showing reduced bacterial burdens in lungs and spleens of treated mice.

claim: The combination therapy with SRT demonstrated enhanced protection in acute TB infection of the highly susceptible C3HeB/FeJ mice.
source: Further, we demonstrate an enhanced protection in acute TB infection of the highly susceptible C3HeB/FeJ mice with the combination therapy signifying the use of SRT as a potent adjunct to standard TB therapeutic regimens against bacterial populations of diverse physiology.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4B-C showing increased mean survival time with SRT combination.

claim: The current TB therapy regimen ranges between 6 months for pulmonary and 1–2 years for extra pulmonary infections.
source: The current TB therapy regimen ranging between 6 months for pulmonary and 1–2 years for extra pulmonary infections, is often associated with severe drug-induced toxicity in patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TB treatment duration.

claim: Current TB therapy is often associated with severe drug-induced toxicity in patients.
source: The current TB therapy regimen ranging between 6 months for pulmonary and 1–2 years for extra pulmonary infections, is often associated with severe drug-induced toxicity in patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TB treatment complications.

claim: Failure of current TB therapy to completely eradicate the pathogen from the host forms an ideal platform for the emergence of drug-resistant strains.
source: Moreover, its failure to completely eradicate the pathogen from the host, forms an ideal platform for the emergence of drug-resistant strains (Blumberg et al., 2003; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drug-resistant TB strains have emerged at an alarming rate in the population.
source: It is not surprising that these strains have emerged at an alarming rate in the population and are imposing serious impediments to TB control programs globally (Falzon et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Host directed therapy (HDT) has the potential to reduce duration of therapy and not be affected by pathogen resistance mechanisms.
source: Introduction of newer modalities like host directed therapy (HDT) with the potential to reduce duration of therapy and not be affected by pathogen resistance mechanisms offer significant advantages in this scenario (Hancock et al., 2012; Munguia and Nizet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on HDT.

claim: Mtb infection invokes several mechanisms of pathogen clearance in host cells involving the induction of pro-inflammatory response, metabolic stress, phago-lysosomal lysis programs, apoptosis/autophagic mechanisms.
source: Mtb infection invokes several mechanisms of pathogen clearance in host cells involving, the induction of pro-inflammatory response, metabolic stress, phago-lysosomal lysis programs, apoptosis/autophagic mechanisms (Benmerzoug et al., 2018; de Martino et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mtb has evolved complex and intricate mechanisms to survive and establish optimal infection in the host.
source: On the other hand, by virtue of its long standing association with humans, Mtb has evolved complex and intricate mechanisms to survive and establish optimal infection in the host (Liu et al., 2017; Padhi et al., 2019; Dey et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2017; Brites and Gagneux, 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2019; Mehta and Singh, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The early, robust, type I IFN response of phagocytes to intracellular bacterial infections including Mtb is often associated with a detrimental effect on host immune activation and survival.
source: The early, robust, type I IFN response of phagocytes to intracellular bacterial infections including Mtb, is often associated with a detrimental effect on host immune activation and survival (Dorhoi et al., 2014; Watson et al., 2015; Donovan et al., 2017; Shankaran et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature including authors' own work.

claim: Sertraline (SRT) is a previously identified antagonist of poly I:C mediated type I IFN signaling in macrophages.
source: We sought to offset this response by using sertraline (SRT) – a previously identified antagonist of poly I:C mediated type I IFN signaling, in macrophages and evaluate Mtb infection dynamics (Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Zhu et al., 2010).

claim: SRT effectively inhibited infection induced IFN that manifested as growth arrest of Mtb in macrophages.
source: We demonstrate that SRT, effectively inhibited infection induced IFN that manifested as growth arrest of Mtb in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1A-C showing IFN inhibition and bacterial growth arrest.

claim: SRT could augment mycobacterial killing in the presence of INH (H) and rifampicin (R) in macrophages by effectively lowering the concentration of antibiotics required to achieve clearance.
source: Interestingly, SRT could augment mycobacterial killing in the presence of INH (H) and rifampicin (R), two of the frontline TB drugs in macrophages by effectively lowering the concentration of antibiotics required to achieve clearance.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1D-E showing enhanced killing at lower antibiotic concentrations with SRT.

claim: The combination of SRT with TB drugs proved effective even against dormant bacilli or antibiotic tolerant Mtb strains.
source: Remarkably, the combination proved effective even against dormant bacilli or antibiotic tolerant Mtb strains.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1G-H (dormant bacilli) and Figure 7 (tolerant strains).

claim: Addition of SRT to TB drugs – HR or HRZE significantly protected infected mice from TB-related pathology both by enhancing bacterial clearance and host survival.
source: Addition of SRT to TB drugs – HR or HRZE (HR +pyrazinamide, ethambutol) significantly protected infected mice from TB-related pathology both by enhancing bacterial clearance and host survival, implying on the usefulness of this combination therapy in both the intensive and continuation phases of anti TB therapy (ATT).
evidence: Supported by in vivo data in Figures 4-6 showing improved survival and reduced bacterial burdens.

claim: SRT controlled Mtb-induced type I IFN response in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The FDA-approved antidepressant – SRT, previously identified to suppress TLR-mediated IRF signaling in macrophages, controlled Mtb-induced type I IFN response in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition.

claim: Extremely low doses of SRT up to 0.5 μM did not alter the type I IFN response.
source: While extremely low doses up to 0.5 μM did not alter the response, doses of 1 μM and higher were significantly inhibitory.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1A showing dose-response relationship.

claim: At 1 µM, SRT inhibited the type I IFN response by 1.5–2 folds.
source: Even at 1 µM, SRT inhibited the response by 1.5–2 folds that increased to 35 and 43%, at 5 μM and 10 μM of SRT, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from Figure 1A.

claim: At 5 μM and 10 μM of SRT, the type I IFN response was inhibited by 35% and 43%, respectively.
source: Even at 1 µM, SRT inhibited the response by 1.5–2 folds that increased to 35 and 43%, at 5 μM and 10 μM of SRT, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from Figure 1A.

claim: At 20 µM, SRT resulted in complete loss of IFNβ secretion by Mtb infected macrophages.
source: At 20 µM, the observed fivefold decrease in RLU SRT reflected as complete loss of IFNβ secretion by Mtb infected macrophages (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1B showing no detectable IFNβ.

claim: Naive macrophages were permissive for Mtb growth to 10-folds of input by day 6.
source: Moreover, while naive macrophages were permissive for Mtb growth to 10-folds of input by day 6, 20 µM of SRT, despite its minimal activity on Mtb in vitro (inhibiting Mtb growth by ~30–40% by days 8–11 of culture), efficiently restricted growth in infected macrophages (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1C.

claim: 20 µM of SRT has minimal activity on Mtb in vitro, inhibiting Mtb growth by ~30–40% by days 8–11 of culture.
source: Moreover, while naive macrophages were permissive for Mtb growth to 10-folds of input by day 6, 20 µM of SRT, despite its minimal activity on Mtb in vitro (inhibiting Mtb growth by ~30–40% by days 8–11 of culture), efficiently restricted growth in infected macrophages (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro growth data referenced in Figure 1C context.

claim: 20 µM of SRT efficiently restricted Mtb growth in infected macrophages.
source: Moreover, while naive macrophages were permissive for Mtb growth to 10-folds of input by day 6, 20 µM of SRT, despite its minimal activity on Mtb in vitro (inhibiting Mtb growth by ~30–40% by days 8–11 of culture), efficiently restricted growth in infected macrophages (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1C showing bacterial stasis.

claim: Decreased portioning of potent antibiotics to regions of bacterial presence in the center of granulomas remains a major cause for the improper clearance of bacteria from infected tissues.
source: Decreased portioning of potent antibiotics to regions of bacterial presence in the center of granulomas remains a major cause for the improper clearance of bacteria from infected tissues (Cicchese et al., 2020; Prideaux et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mtb is endowed with the inherent propensity to enter into a drug-tolerant, non-replicating dormant state associated with drug tolerance and antibiotic failure.
source: In addition, Mtb is endowed with the inherent propensity to enter into a drug-tolerant, non-replicating dormant state associated with drug tolerance and antibiotic failure (Sarathy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: C1 concentration (200 ng/ml INH and 1000 ng/ml Rifampicin) was able to reduce bacterial numbers drastically (~62-fold by day 3 and ~92-fold by day 5).
source: As expected, a gradual reduction in antibiotic effectivity was observed with decreasing doses; while C1 (200 ng/ml INH and 1000 ng/ml Rifampicin) was able to reduce bacterial numbers drastically (~62-fold by day 3 and ~92-fold by day 5), a 10-fold lower dose of C2 (20 ng/ml INH and 100 ng/ml Rifampicin) was less effective resulting in with 2–3 folds lower numbers and bacteriostasis in cells treated with the 2.5-fold lower dose -C3-8 ng/ml INH and 40 ng/ml Rifampicin (similar to input values) (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1D.

claim: C2 concentration (20 ng/ml INH and 100 ng/ml Rifampicin) was less effective resulting in 2–3 folds lower bacterial numbers.
source: As expected, a gradual reduction in antibiotic effectivity was observed with decreasing doses; while C1 (200 ng/ml INH and 1000 ng/ml Rifampicin) was able to reduce bacterial numbers drastically (~62-fold by day 3 and ~92-fold by day 5), a 10-fold lower dose of C2 (20 ng/ml INH and 100 ng/ml Rifampicin) was less effective resulting in with 2–3 folds lower numbers and bacteriostasis in cells treated with the 2.5-fold lower dose -C3-8 ng/ml INH and 40 ng/ml Rifampicin (similar to input values) (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1E.

claim: C3 concentration (8 ng/ml INH and 40 ng/ml Rifampicin) resulted in bacteriostasis with bacterial numbers similar to input values.
source: As expected, a gradual reduction in antibiotic effectivity was observed with decreasing doses; while C1 (200 ng/ml INH and 1000 ng/ml Rifampicin) was able to reduce bacterial numbers drastically (~62-fold by day 3 and ~92-fold by day 5), a 10-fold lower dose of C2 (20 ng/ml INH and 100 ng/ml Rifampicin) was less effective resulting in with 2–3 folds lower numbers and bacteriostasis in cells treated with the 2.5-fold lower dose -C3-8 ng/ml INH and 40 ng/ml Rifampicin (similar to input values) (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1E.

claim: Addition of SRT efficiently boosted the bactericidal properties of antibiotics at all concentrations tested.
source: Addition of SRT efficiently boosted the bactericidal properties of antibiotics at all concentrations tested.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1D-E showing enhanced killing across all antibiotic concentrations.

claim: At the highly effective HR concentration (C1), addition of SRT further reduced bacterial numbers by 2–3 folds.
source: Even at the highly effective HR concentration, addition of SRT further reduced bacterial numbers by 2–3 folds (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1D.

claim: At the C2 dose, SRT lowered bacterial numbers by 8-fold at day 3 and 50-fold by day 5.
source: Surprisingly, the ability of SRT to boost antibiotic properties was evident at lower doses- at the C2 dose, SRT lowered numbers by 8 at day 3 and 50 folds by day 5.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1E.

claim: At the lowest dose of C3, SRT substantially enhanced bacterial killing by 6-fold at day 3 and 20-fold at day 5 in comparison to HR.
source: Even at the lowest dose of C3, SRT substantially enhanced bacterial killing by 6- and 20-folds at days 3 and 5 post infection, respectively, in comparison to HR (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1E.

claim: The antibiotic potentiating effect of SRT was preserved in primary macrophages from seven healthy individuals.
source: This ability of SRT was also observed in primary macrophages (human monocyte derived macrophages) from seven healthy individuals. Although Mtb growth varied across samples, the antibiotic potentiating effect of SRT was preserved (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by CFU data from primary human macrophages in Figure 1F.

claim: SRT universally synergized with antibiotics to further reduce bacterial numbers by 10–15 folds across different individuals.
source: Across different individuals, while SRT and HR individually showed minimal but highly variable bacterial control, SRT universally synergized with antibiotics to further reduce bacterial numbers by 10–15 folds supporting a more general adjunct activity of SRT to frontline TB drugs.
evidence: Supported by CFU data from primary human macrophages in Figure 1F.

claim: HR efficacy was completely nullified in macrophages with vitamin C pretreatment.
source: Again, while HR efficacy was completely nullified in macrophages with vitamin C pretreatment, inclusion of SRT resulted in 10–12-fold lower bacterial numbers after 4 days of treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1G showing loss of HR efficacy in vitamin C-treated cells.

claim: Inclusion of SRT resulted in 10–12-fold lower bacterial numbers after 4 days of treatment in vitamin C-treated macrophages.
source: Again, while HR efficacy was completely nullified in macrophages with vitamin C pretreatment, inclusion of SRT resulted in 10–12-fold lower bacterial numbers after 4 days of treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1G.

claim: The combination of H and R showed poor efficacy in controlling infection in lipid-loaded macrophages.
source: In order to mimic lipid rich conditions in ex vivo studies, we treated THP1 macrophages with 200 µM oleic acid and observed significant lipid loading in cells without any alteration in cellular morphology. However, the combination of H and R showed poor efficacy in controlling infection, from and found poor efficiency of HR in these cells, addition of SRT led to more than 10-fold reduction in bacterial loads, further substantiating the increased bactericidal properties of the combination (HRS) in conditions of decreased antibiotic efficacy (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1H showing poor HR efficacy in lipid-rich conditions.

claim: Addition of SRT led to more than 10-fold reduction in bacterial loads in lipid-loaded macrophages.
source: In order to mimic lipid rich conditions in ex vivo studies, we treated THP1 macrophages with 200 µM oleic acid and observed significant lipid loading in cells without any alteration in cellular morphology. However, the combination of H and R showed poor efficacy in controlling infection, from and found poor efficiency of HR in these cells, addition of SRT led to more than 10-fold reduction in bacterial loads, further substantiating the increased bactericidal properties of the combination (HRS) in conditions of decreased antibiotic efficacy (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 1H.

claim: SRT increased HR efficiency in a dose dependent manner with doses lower than 1 µM failing to alter the growth of Mtb in macrophages.
source: Similar to the type I IFN response restriction, SRT was found to increase HR efficiency in a dose dependent manner with doses lower than 1 µM failing to alter the growth of Mtb in macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At concentration of 1–20 µM, SRT could effectively synergize with antibiotics and inhibit bacterial numbers by ~5–70 folds, respectively, in the treated macrophages.
source: At concentration of 1–20 µM, SRT, could effectively synergize with antibiotics and inhibit bacterial numbers by ~5–70 folds, respectively, in the treated macrophages (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2A showing dose-dependent synergy.

claim: SRT along with HR does not significantly inhibit Mtb growth in vitro.
source: However, SRT along with HR does not significantly inhibit growth in vitro, even 6 μM SRT failed to impact Mtb growth either alone or in combination with 3 concentrations of HR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), alluding to an indirect mode of SRT in enhancing the ability of macrophages to control bacteria rather than a direct action on bacteria.
evidence: Supported by in vitro growth data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SRT enhances the ability of macrophages to control bacteria through an indirect mode rather than a direct action on bacteria.
source: However, SRT along with HR does not significantly inhibit growth in vitro, even 6 μM SRT failed to impact Mtb growth either alone or in combination with 3 concentrations of HR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), alluding to an indirect mode of SRT in enhancing the ability of macrophages to control bacteria rather than a direct action on bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of direct antimicrobial activity in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) combined with efficacy in macrophages.

claim: BX795 at concentrations as low as 1.2 μM completely nullified the infection induced type I IFN response in macrophages.
source: We first established the efficacy of BX795 in abrogating Mtb-induced type I IFN in THP1 macrophages at different concentrations. Treatment of macrophages with BX795 at concentrations as low as 1.2 μM completely nullified the infection induced type I IFN response in macrophages (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2B.

claim: BX795 alone resulted in bacteriostasis with bacterial numbers maintained at input levels in macrophages.
source: Again, similar to SRT, BX795 alone resulted in bacteriostasis with bacterial numbers maintained at input levels in these cells in similar to SRT treated macrophages (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2C.

claim: Addition of BX795 to HR enhanced bacterial control by 4–5 folds by day 3 of infection as compared to the antibiotics alone.
source: Again, addition of BX795 to HR enhanced bacterial control by 4–5 folds by day 3 of infection as compared to the antibiotics alone (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2D.

claim: Nearly 2–3 folds lower bacterial numbers were observed in cGAS-/- macrophages compared to WT cells after 3 days of treatment with HR.
source: As expected, Mtb was restricted in its growth in these macrophages. Nearly 2–3 folds lower bacterial numbers were observed in cGAS-/- (Figure 2E) with a much stronger inhibition (40–50 folds) in STING-/- macrophages (Figure 2F) in comparison to the corresponding IFN-sufficient cells.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2E comparing cGAS-/- to WT macrophages.

claim: 40–50 folds lower bacterial numbers were observed in STING-/- macrophages compared to WT cells after 3 days of treatment with HR.
source: As expected, Mtb was restricted in its growth in these macrophages. Nearly 2–3 folds lower bacterial numbers were observed in cGAS-/- (Figure 2E) with a much stronger inhibition (40–50 folds) in STING-/- macrophages (Figure 2F) in comparison to the corresponding IFN-sufficient cells.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2F comparing STING-/- to WT macrophages.

claim: Elaboration of a pro-inflammatory response is one of the potent responses with activation of anti-mycobactericidal activities in macrophages.
source: Elaboration of a pro-inflammatory response is one of the potent responses with activation of anti-mycobactericidal activities in macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macrophage immune responses.

claim: IFNγ treatment resulted in two- to threefold lower bacteria in combination with HR alone.
source: While IFNγ treatment resulted in two- to threefold lower bacteria in combination with HR alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found a similar enhancement in IFNγ mediated control in SRT-treated macrophages (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene expression profiles showed reduction in the expression of TNF and IL1β after 18 hr of treatment with SRT.
source: Gene expression profiles showed reduction in the expression of TNF and IL1β after 18 hr of treatment with SRT consistent with reported literature (Figure 3B–E; Sitges et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3B and 3D, and citation to previous literature.

claim: Negligible levels of TNF was observed in the cell supernatants in SRT-treated cells (SRT, HRS).
source: In comparison to HR, while TNF expression was reduced slightly in the HRS-treated macrophages (Figure 3B), negligible levels of TNF was observed in the cell supernatants in SRT-treated cells (SRT, HRS), contrasting with the high levels of TNF (between 500pg- 1 ng/ml) in the case of Mtb infected cells with or without treatment with HR (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3C.

claim: High levels of TNF (between 500pg- 1 ng/ml) were observed in Mtb infected cells with or without treatment with HR.
source: In comparison to HR, while TNF expression was reduced slightly in the HRS-treated macrophages (Figure 3B), negligible levels of TNF was observed in the cell supernatants in SRT-treated cells (SRT, HRS), contrasting with the high levels of TNF (between 500pg- 1 ng/ml) in the case of Mtb infected cells with or without treatment with HR (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression levels of IL1β were 2–3 folds lower in HRS-treated macrophages by 18 hr.
source: Surprisingly, while expression levels of IL1β were 2–3 folds lower in HRS-treated macrophages by 18 hr (Figure 3D), the amount of secreted cytokine was significantly elevated (>2–3 folds) in macrophages treated with SRT/ HRS from 18 hr until 66 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3D.

claim: The amount of secreted IL1β was significantly elevated (>2–3 folds) in macrophages treated with SRT/ HRS from 18 hr until 66 hr.
source: Surprisingly, while expression levels of IL1β were 2–3 folds lower in HRS-treated macrophages by 18 hr (Figure 3D), the amount of secreted cytokine was significantly elevated (>2–3 folds) in macrophages treated with SRT/ HRS from 18 hr until 66 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3E.

claim: The data strongly indicated potential activation of the host cell inflammasome by SRT.
source: These data strongly indicated potential activation of the host cell inflammasome by SRT.
evidence: Inferred from the elevated IL1β secretion despite reduced transcription, which is characteristic of inflammasome activation.

claim: Several studies support inverse regulation of type I IFN and inflammasome activation.
source: With several studies supporting inverse regulation of type I IFN and inflammasome activation (Szałach et al., 2019; Ruiz-Grosso et al., 2020), we tested the efficacy of SRT to potentiate antibiotic mediated killing in the presence of inflammasome inhibitors- isoliquiritigenin (I) and MCC950.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Isoliquiritigenin did not show any significant effect on macrophages that were untreated or treated with HR or SRT alone.
source: Isoliquiritigenin did not show any significant effect on macrophages that were untreated or treated with HR or SRT alone (Figure 3F, inset).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 3F inset.

claim: Addition of SRT to HR significantly reduced bacterial numbers in macrophages by more than 10–20 folds.
source: However, while addition of SRT to HR significantly reduced bacterial numbers in macrophages by more than 10–20 folds, pretreatment of cells with the isoliquiritigenin, completely nullified this boosting effect of SRT on antibiotic efficacy (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 3F.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with isoliquiritigenin completely nullified the boosting effect of SRT on antibiotic efficacy.
source: However, while addition of SRT to HR significantly reduced bacterial numbers in macrophages by more than 10–20 folds, pretreatment of cells with the isoliquiritigenin, completely nullified this boosting effect of SRT on antibiotic efficacy (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 3F showing loss of SRT synergy with inflammasome inhibitor.

claim: Treatment with MCC950 resulted in a reversal of enhanced bacterial control in HRS in infected macrophages without altering the effect of antibiotics alone.
source: Treatment with a NLRP3-specific inhibitor- MCC950 also resulted in a reversal of enhanced bacterial control in HRS in infected macrophages without altering the effect of antibiotics alone on the bactericidal properties validating the involvement of inflammasome in the ability of SRT to enhance bacterial control by frontline antibiotics.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 3G showing loss of SRT synergy with NLRP3 inhibitor.

claim: A significant decrease in Mtb-induced type I IFN in macrophages was observed following treatment with inflammasome activation.
source: In line with previous studies (Labzin et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2018), we also observed a significant decrease in Mtb-induced type I IFN in macrophages following treatment with inflammasome activation (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3H and citations to previous literature.

claim: Treatment with SRT and HR significantly reduced type I IFN response in macrophages.
source: While treatment with SRT and HR significantly reduced this response in macrophages, pretreatment with the inflammasome inhibitor- MCC950 partially reversed this decline again arguing for an important role for inflammasome activation in the type I IFN modulating effect of SRT.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3H.

claim: Pretreatment with the inflammasome inhibitor MCC950 partially reversed the decline in type I IFN response caused by SRT and HR.
source: While treatment with SRT and HR significantly reduced this response in macrophages, pretreatment with the inflammasome inhibitor- MCC950 partially reversed this decline again arguing for an important role for inflammasome activation in the type I IFN modulating effect of SRT.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3H showing partial reversal with MCC950.

claim: Aerosol delivery at 500 CFU dose resulted in precipitous disease with rapid killing of untreated (NT) animals by day 31 of infection.
source: Aerosol delivery at this dose resulted in precipitous disease with rapid killing of untreated (NT) animals by day 31 of infection (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4B.

claim: SRT alone was effective in delaying the disease progression in animals as the mean survival time (MST) increased from 31 days for untreated animals to 38 days.
source: SRT alone was effective in delaying the disease progression in animals as the mean survival time (MST) increased from 31 days for untreated animals to 38 days.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: HR at the lowest concentration (C3) deferred animal mortality with MST of 41 days.
source: HR at the lowest concentration (C3), similar to SRT, deferred animal mortality with MST of 41 days while the higher doses of HR (C2 and C1) increased MST significantly to 85 and >90, respectively.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Higher doses of HR (C2 and C1) increased MST significantly to 85 and >90 days, respectively.
source: HR at the lowest concentration (C3), similar to SRT, deferred animal mortality with MST of 41 days while the higher doses of HR (C2 and C1) increased MST significantly to 85 and >90, respectively.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The combination of HRC3 and SRT nearly doubled the MST of both female and male mice to 78 days and 100 days from 41 and 45 days respectively.
source: The combination of HRC3 and SRT, nearly doubled the MST of both female and male mice to 78 days and 100 days from 41 and 45 days respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4C showing gender-specific MST values.

claim: The benefit of SRT was similar to that observed for a 10-fold higher concentration of HR alone (MST of 85 for HRC2).
source: This benefit of SRT was similar to that observed for a 10-fold higher concentration of HR alone (MST of 85 for HRC2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of survival data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Both NT and HRC3 treated lungs showed extensive progressive granulomas by 30 days of infection.
source: The advantage of SRT inclusion with HR was evident in the gross lung pathology by 30 days of infection. Both NT and HRC3 treated lungs showed extensive progressive granulomas, contrasting with a significant amelioration of pathology seen in HRC3 +S treated animals (scale bars of 0.1mm) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by gross pathology images in Figure 4D.

claim: HRC3 +S treated animals showed a significant amelioration of pathology by 30 days of infection.
source: The advantage of SRT inclusion with HR was evident in the gross lung pathology by 30 days of infection. Both NT and HRC3 treated lungs showed extensive progressive granulomas, contrasting with a significant amelioration of pathology seen in HRC3 +S treated animals (scale bars of 0.1mm) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by gross pathology images in Figure 4D.

claim: 100% of animals survived after treatment with HR(C1) at 16 weeks post infection.
source: In this model, 100% of animals survived after treatment with HR(C1) at 16 weeks post infection (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: A 7 week ad libitum treatment with the 10-fold lower dose of HR (HRC2) significantly decreased the MST of animals to 85 days with 100% mortality by 16 weeks.
source: A 7 week ad libitum treatment with the 10-fold lower dose of HR (HRC2) (Figure 4F) significantly decreased the MST of animals to 85 days with 100% mortality by 16 weeks.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: 40% of HRC2S-treated animals survived with a MST of 112 days for the group.
source: In contrast, 40% of HRC2S-treated animals, survived with a MST of 112 days for the group (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4F-G.

claim: All animals with the highest dose of HR (HRC1) either alone or with SRT survived the infection.
source: All animals with the highest dose of HR (HRC1) either alone or with SRT survived the infection.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: Small macroscopic lesions were observed in lungs of 60% of the female mice treated with HRC1 that showed as multiple, well-defined granuloma in the H&E-stained sections by the 16th week post infection.
source: Small macroscopic lesions were observed in lungs of 60% of the female mice treated with HRC1 that showed as multiple, well-defined granuloma in the H&E-stained sections by the 16th week post infection.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 4H.

claim: Mice treated with SRT and HRC1 showed negligible involvement of the lung tissue in granulomatous cellular accumulation.
source: In contrast, mice treated with SRT and HRC1 showed negligible involvement of the lung tissue in granulomatous cellular accumulation.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 4H.

claim: Male animals receiving the adjunct therapy showed fewer macroscopic and significantly lower numbers of microscopic granuloma in lung sections in comparison to animals treated with the antibiotics alone.
source: Even in tissues of male mice, animals receiving the adjunct therapy showed fewer macroscopic and significantly lower numbers of microscopic granuloma in lung sections in comparison to animals treated with the antibiotics alone.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 4H and lesion counts in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Male and female animals treated with the 4 drugs for 7 weeks harbored 105–106 bacteria in their lungs, respectively.
source: Male (Figure 5B) and female (Figure 5C) animals treated with the 4 drugs for 7 weeks harbored 105–106 bacteria in their lungs, respectively.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Addition of SRT appreciably improved drug efficacy, reducing the lung bacterial loads by a further 5–7 folds.
source: Addition of SRT appreciably improved drug efficacy, reducing the lung bacterial loads by a further 5–7 folds (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Animals treated with HRZES were devoid of granulomatous infiltrates in contrast to the HRZE treated animals which had significantly higher numbers of granulomas in the lungs.
source: This difference was more evident in tissue sections, wherein animals treated with HRZES were devoid of granulomatous infiltrates in contrast to the HRZE treated animals which had significantly higher numbers of granulomas in the lungs (Scale bars of 0.1mm)(Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 5D.

claim: Bacterial numbers in the lungs reached ~107 CFU by 4 weeks of infection (day 0 of treatment) and remained steady over the 6-week period in untreated animals.
source: Bacterial numbers in the lungs reached ~107 CFU by 4 weeks of infection (day 0 of treatment) and remained steady over the 6-week period in untreated animals.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with HRZE was efficient in steadily reducing bacterial numbers by ~100 folds.
source: While treatment with HRZE was efficient in steadily reducing these numbers by ~100 folds, addition of SRT to the regimen significantly enhanced control by a further 2–3 folds.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6B.

claim: Addition of SRT to the regimen significantly enhanced control by a further 2–3 folds.
source: While treatment with HRZE was efficient in steadily reducing these numbers by ~100 folds, addition of SRT to the regimen significantly enhanced control by a further 2–3 folds.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6B.

claim: HRZE reduced splenic bacterial numbers significantly by 6–7 folds.
source: Although HRZE reduced splenic bacterial numbers significantly by 6–7 folds, HRZES was more potent reducing bacterial numbers further by ~20 folds (60–70% vs ~2–5%) by 21 days of treatment (Figure 6B, inset).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6B inset.

claim: HRZES was more potent reducing bacterial numbers further by ~20 folds (60–70% vs ~2–5%) by 21 days of treatment in spleens.
source: Although HRZE reduced splenic bacterial numbers significantly by 6–7 folds, HRZES was more potent reducing bacterial numbers further by ~20 folds (60–70% vs ~2–5%) by 21 days of treatment (Figure 6B, inset).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6B inset.

claim: A similar degree of enhanced bacterial control (4–6 folds lesser bacteria) was observed in lungs and spleens of Balb/c mice treated with SRT as an adjunct to conventional 4 drug-therapy.
source: A similar degree of enhanced bacterial control (4–6 folds lesser bacteria) was observed in lungs and spleens of Balb/c mice treated with SRT as an adjunct to conventional 4 drug-therapy (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with HRZE was efficient in reducing cellular infiltration significantly by the 6th week of infection with nearly 1/6th of the tissue showing signs of cellular infiltration.
source: Treatment with HRZE was efficient in reducing this infiltration significantly by the 6th week of infection with nearly 1/6th of the tissue showing signs of cellular infiltration (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 6C.

claim: Lungs of mice receiving the combination showed better resolution of granulomas with significantly smaller regions of cellular collection by 3 weeks dispersed across the tissue, that was more or less absent from the tissues of mice by the 6th week of treatment.
source: Lungs of mice receiving the combination showed better resolution of granulomas with significantly smaller regions of cellular collection by 3 weeks dispersed across the tissue, that was more or less absent from the tissues of mice by the 6th week of treatment.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment with HRZE for up to 8 weeks did not effectively clear the bacterial from the lungs of infected mice.
source: Treatment with HRZE for up to 8 weeks did not effectively clear the bacterial from the lungs of infected mice (scale bar of 0.1mm). While untreated animals harbored close to 106 bacilli in the lungs, all treated mice had between 40 and 640 bacteria in the lungs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6D showing residual bacteria after 8 weeks of treatment.

claim: All treated mice had between 40 and 640 bacteria in the lungs after 8 weeks of HRZE treatment.
source: Treatment with HRZE for up to 8 weeks did not effectively clear the bacterial from the lungs of infected mice (scale bar of 0.1mm). While untreated animals harbored close to 106 bacilli in the lungs, all treated mice had between 40 and 640 bacteria in the lungs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6D.

claim: Addition of SRT resulted in the absence of countable bacteria in lungs of 4/5 mice with one animal having 40 bacteria.
source: In contrast addition of SRT, resulted in the absence of countable bacteria in lungs of 4/5 mice with one animal having 40 bacteria, similar to the animal with the best resolution of infection by the HRZE treated animals.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6D showing sterilization in most animals.

claim: The spleens of animals receiving the combination treatment did not show any detectable bacteria as opposed to the frontline TB drugs alone.
source: Even the spleens of animals receiving the combination treatment did not show any detectable bacteria as opposed to the frontline TB drugs alone substantiating the ability of SRT to impart early bacterial clearance from animal tissues in comparison to the standard 4 TB drugs (Figure 6D, inset).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6D inset.

claim: Mtb persisted in animals given HRZE showing countable colonies in both lungs and spleen (2 out of 3 animals) at 9 weeks post treatment.
source: Further evidence of faster clearance was evident at 9 weeks post treatment and even at lower doses of SRT. While Mtb persisted in animals given HRZE showing countable colonies in both lungs and spleen (2 out of 3 animals), the combination of SRT was successful in eliminating bacteria from animal tissues at the doses of 3 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6E.

claim: The combination of SRT was successful in eliminating bacteria from animal tissues at the doses of 3 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg.
source: Further evidence of faster clearance was evident at 9 weeks post treatment and even at lower doses of SRT. While Mtb persisted in animals given HRZE showing countable colonies in both lungs and spleen (2 out of 3 animals), the combination of SRT was successful in eliminating bacteria from animal tissues at the doses of 3 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6E showing complete clearance at higher SRT doses.

claim: SRT doses as low as 0.125 mg/kg was sufficient to clear bacterial loads in spleen from animals.
source: Interestingly SRT doses as low as 0.125 mg/kg was sufficient to clear bacterial loads in spleen from animals (Figure 6E, inset), the bacterial numbers in the lungs were more or less similar to the numbers in the HRZE group.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6E inset.

claim: At doses of 0.5mgkg and 1mgkg, SRT was more effective in controlling bacteria in the spleens and lungs of mice as compared to the HRZE group.
source: Even at doses of 0.5mgkg and 1mgkg, SRT was more effective in controlling bacteria in the spleens and lungs of mice as compared to the HRZE group, again validating that the combination imparted faster in vivo bacterial clearance.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 6E.

claim: N73 is a clinical Mtb strain belonging to the L1 ancient lineage that showed increasing tolerance to INH and Rifampicin as opposed to the modern L3 and L4 lineage strains by virtue of expressing the complete MmpL6 operon.
source: Previously, we had demonstrated that N73- a clinical Mtb strain belonging to the L1 ancient lineage showed increasing tolerance to INH and Rifampicin as opposed to the modern L3 and L4 lineage strains by virtue of expressing the complete MmpL6 operon (Arumugam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work.

claim: In THP1 cells infected with N73 Mtb, HR at C2 concentration supported stasis and failed to decrease bacterial numbers.
source: In THP1 cells infected with Mtb, HR at C2 concentration supported stasis and failed to decrease of bacterial numbers (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7A showing lack of HR efficacy against N73 strain.

claim: The combination of HR with SRT significantly controlled N73 infection and reduced bacterial numbers by ~10–15 folds by 3 days and ~100 folds by day 5.
source: The combination of HR with SRT, significantly controlled infection and reduced bacterial numbers by ~10–15 folds by 3 days and ~100 folds by day5.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7A.

claim: A combination of HR and SRT reduced intracellular N73 bacterial numbers by 5–50 folds in comparison to the drugs alone in primary human macrophages.
source: The pattern of significantly greater bacterial control was also observed in primary human macrophages; again, a combination of HR and SRT reduced intracellular bacterial numbers by 5–50 folds in comparison to the drugs alone (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7B from primary human macrophages.

claim: HR reduced bacterial numbers by fivefolds in C3HeB/FeJ mice infected with N73 strain.
source: As expected, the drugs were not efficient in controlling infection induced lesions in the lungs reducing bacterial numbers by fivefolds (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7D.

claim: Lungs of HRS treated animals harbored ~5–8 folds lower bacterial numbers than HR treated animals in N73 infection.
source: However, lungs of HRS treated animals harbored ~5–8 folds lower bacterial numbers than HR treated animals.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7D.

claim: HR did not reduce CFU in spleens of N73-infected mice in contrast to the six- to eightfold lower bacterial numbers with the HRS combination.
source: The effect of the combination was again better in controlling bacterial numbers in spleens of treated mice wherein HR did not reduce CFU in contrast to the six- to eightfold lower bacterial numbers with the combination.
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 7D.

claim: SRT, along with other weak bases like fluoxetine, has been reported to moderately restrict intracellular Mtb replication in macrophages due in part to its weak basic nature without affecting the host cell viability.
source: SRT, along with other weak bases like fluoxetine, has been reported to moderately restrict intracellular Mtb replication in macrophages due in part to its weak basic nature without affecting the host cell viability (Schump et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: An important role for the acidic environment of bacteria resident vesicles (pH dependence) in the mycobactericidal properties of weak base drugs was demonstrated.
source: An important role for the acidic environment of bacteria resident vesicles (pH dependence) in the mycobactericidal properties of these drugs was demonstrated in this study.
evidence: Refers to findings from the Schump et al., 2017 study cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Several studies have indicated a direct action of SRT and other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors on host immune response pathways.
source: Additionally, several studies have indicated a direct action of SRT and other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors on host immune response pathways: from enhancing the anti-inflammatory response (Hannestad et al., 2011), augmenting NK and CD8 cell response (Benton et al., 2010) and to inhibition of acid-sphingomyelinase (Kouznetsova et al., 2014), an essential component of the viral trafficking into NPC1 +endosomes in cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of host cell inflammasome and its antagonistic effect on the type I IFN response of cells has now been realized as important factors for controlling bacterial infections.
source: Activation of host cell inflammasome and its antagonistic effect on the type I IFN response of cells has now been realized as important factors for controlling bacterial infections (Novikov et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A direct effect on activating eicosanoids which control type I IFN following infection was identified as a key bacterial clearance mechanism of infected cells.
source: A direct effect on activating eicosanoids which control type I IFN following infection was identified as a key bacterial clearance mechanism of infected cells (Hawn et al., 2015; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Targeted therapy toward elevating PGE2 activity protected mice from acute infection-induced fatality.
source: Consistent with this observation, targeted therapy toward elevating PGE2 activity protected mice from acute infection-induced fatality (Mayer-Barber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The pharmacological properties of SRT with excellent PK-PD, safety and tolerance for long term usage in the human population has been well established.
source: The pharmacological properties of SRT with excellent PK-PD, safety and tolerance for long term usage in the human population has been well established (Sheehan and Kamijima, 2009; Ronfeld et al., 1997; Mandrioli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on sertraline pharmacology.

claim: Two patients undergoing TB therapy with INH given SRT as an anti-depressant did not show any deleterious effects on long-term use of the combination.
source: Interestingly, two patients undergoing TB therapy with INH given SRT as an anti- depressant, did not show any deleterious effects on long-term use of the combination, auguring well for safety in the human population (Malek-Ahmadi et al., 1996; Judd et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to case reports.

claim: A recent clinical trial with SRT as an adjunct regimen with fluconazole for asymptomatic cryptococcal antigenemia demonstrated SAEs (non-fatal) in 4 out of 10 participants.
source: A recent clinical trial with SRT as an adjunct regimen with fluconazole for asymptomatic cryptococcal antigenemia demonstrated SAEs (non-fatal) in 4 out of 10 participants (3 with psychosis and aggressive behavioral changes, 1 with serotonin syndrome) as opposed to 3 out of 10 (1 fatal) SAEs in the control placebo group (Boulware et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a clinical trial.

claim: SRT may be beneficial in tackling the dual problem of severe drug induced depression in TB patients.
source: While such concerns cannot be overlooked for use of SRT as an adjunct TB therapy, it would be prudent to weigh the advantages of the tackling the dual problem of severe drug induced depression in TB patients (invisible co-morbidity) (Sweetland et al., 2017; Trenton and Currier, 2001) in future detailed studies on the effective dose and duration of therapy needs to be undertaken.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on depression in TB patients.
